newsitem.title: USA: Dow Corning creditors propose $2.95 billion plan.
newsitem.headline: Dow Corning creditors propose $2.95 billion plan.

text.p: Women suing Dow Corning Corp. for alleged harm from the company's silicone breast implants and the company's creditors proposed Friday that Dow Corning provide about $2.95 billion to settle their claims.

The agreement between the plaintiffs and creditors challenges Dow Corning's own $3 billion reorganization plan to emerge from Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, under which it has been operating since May 1995.

The groups said in a joint statement that they agreed on principal terms and conditions for the rival reorganization plan and on Friday sought approval from the U.S. Bankruptcy Court in Bay City, Mich. to file their joint plan.

Dow Corning, a joint venture between Dow Chemical Co. and Corning Inc., would emerge from bankruptcy in 12 months under the plan, they said. Once the world's largest maker of breast implants, the company stopped making the products after thousands of women sued it for alleged health problems after receiving silicone gel breast implants.
Dow Corning maintains the implants did not cause disease.

The plan calls for Dow Corning to set up a trust with an initial $1.75 billion to resolve and pay product liability claims by women who charge that the company's silicon implants caused injury and for other silicon implant related cases.
Additional funds would be needed if Dow Corning were to be held liable for claims that silicon implants caused disease.
Another $1.2 billion would be provided to compensate commercial claims, the groups said.

The plan was drawn up by the Commercial Creditors' Committee, which represents all of Dow Corning's financial and trade creditors, and the Tort Claimants' Committee of Dow Corning, which represents women with breast implants, as well as others who have asserted injuries from medical implants.

"The Joint Committee motion represents a giant step forward in fairly and promptly resolving this 18 month bankruptcy case," said Sybil Niden Goldrich, a member of the Tort Committee negotiating team.

"The plan is designed to permit Dow Corning to emerge from bankruptcy, pay its commercial debt, and make a reasonable initial payment to implant recipients within the next 12 months, while preserving the rights of the company and implant claimants to fully litigate the issue of breast implants and disease."
The groups criticised Dow Corning's plan, which was announced in December, characterising it as a "last minute response" to the committees' anticipated filing of their joint motion.
The groups agreed on their plan after "hundreds of hours of negotiations," said Frederick Moryl of Banque Nationale de Paris, chairman of the Commercial Committee.
"The joint plan is designed to achieve an overall consensus in the case but, if necessary, can move forward even without the support of Dow Corning or its shareholders," he said.
Moryl said Dow Corning's plan was "not based on meaningful negotiations over the treatment of tort claims" and merely adopts the "litigation positions" that the company has taken throughout the case.
"Unless the committees are permitted to present their plan, the bankruptcy is likely to remain bogged down in litigation and endless delays," Moryl said.
A Dow Corning spokeswoman, Barbara Muessig, said the company had not yet seen the creditors' plan.
However, she said the company still favoured its own reorganization plan, which seeks to determine up front if breast implants cause disease.

"We can't get through bankruptcy without resolving the issue of whether the breast implants led to disease," she said. Earlier this week, a Dow Corning spokesman said the company believed it would take 12 to 18 months to emerge from bankrputcy.
